content: Iodine monochloride is a chemical compound with the molecular formula ICl. It appears as a red-brown substance and has a melting point close to room temperature. The preparation of iodine monochloride involves a straightforward reaction where iodine and chlorine are combined in a 1:1 molar ratio. When chlorine gas is passed over solid iodine crystals, the reaction produces brown vapors of iodine monochloride. The resulting dark brown liquid iodine monochloride is then collected. If excess chlorine is introduced, iodine monochloride can be converted into iodine trichloride through a reversible reaction. Polymorphism, a phenomenon where a solid can exist in multiple crystalline forms, is observed in iodine monochloride. One of its polymorphic forms has a melting point of 9°C. Iodine monochloride is a valuable reagent in organic synthesis. It serves as a source of electrophilic iodine, which is used to synthesize specific aromatic iodides. Additionally, it can cleave carbon-silicon (C-Si) bonds. Iodine monochloride also reacts with alkenes by adding across the double bond to form chloro-iodo alkanes. When these reactions are carried out in the presence of sodium azide, the product is an iodo-azide compound, with the general structure RCH(I)-CH(N3)R'.
